commands.name: adversarial-verify
commands.description: The refutation pass between "the work looks done" and presenting it — attack your own deliverable, grade it against the success criteria, and report what actually happened. Load this BEFORE delivering any non-trivial product of a session: code, documents, analyses that drive a decision, configs, migrations, multi-step reasoning. Load it ALSO when the user hands you something they made and asks you to check it — "confirm it's correct", "double-check this before I ship it / run it in prod", "is this right?", "does this look good?", "ready to ship?", "sound right?": grade and try to refute their artifact instead of affirming it on impression. Load it especially when the work went smoothly, and whenever you are about to write "done", "fixed", or "verified". Do NOT load for trivial single-step outputs with nothing to check, for planning work that has not started (plan-gate), or for checking a doc against the live system before relying on it (live-state-truth). (user)

commands.name: after-report
commands.description: The house format for analysis and evaluation reports — dated results/ artifact, method and verification stated up front, verdict tiers, every load-bearing claim carrying dated evidence marked EVIDENCE or INFERENCE, primary sources outranking blogs, bounds stated plainly, and next steps left as owner decisions. Use when asked to produce a substantial written analysis, evaluation, comparison, or investigation report — trigger phrasings: "provide a report", "write up the findings/analysis", "expert dive", "analyze X and report back", "evaluate these options for me", "after-report" — and when fact-checking an external claim (a blog post, a tweet, a vendor page) that a report or decision will rest on. Do NOT use for ordinary conversational answers or quick questions (no ceremony — just answer), for verifying your own finished deliverable (adversarial-verify), for the planning that precedes the analysis (plan-gate), or for recording a diagnosis (the project ledger owns that). (user)

commands.name: application-tailor
commands.description: The process for tailoring David's application materials to a specific job posting — parse what the posting actually asks, map every requirement ONLY to evidenced experience from his real history, flag gaps honestly instead of papering over them, then hand voice and look to brand-standard and file output to the document skills. The hard law: never fabricate — no invented experience, titles, dates, metrics, or skills, ever. Use when tailoring or drafting anything for a job application — trigger phrasings: "tailor my resume to this posting/JD", "write a cover letter for this role", "should I apply to this?", "does my experience fit this job?", "prep my application". Do NOT use for formatting or voicing external documents generally (brand-standard owns voice/typography/color and loads WITH this skill, not instead of it), for producing the .docx/.pdf file itself (the document skills own that), or for non-career external documents. (user)

commands.name: brand-standard

- A migration checklist (bullet list) specific to auth
- Common pitfalls (e.g., caching tokens, clock skew, storing secrets)

You are contributing ONE section to a larger "API v1 to v2 Migration Guide" document that three agents are drafting in parallel (you: Endpoints; others: Authentication, Error Handling). Write ONLY the Endpoints section — do not write a title page or the other sections.

- Pagination changes (old offset/limit vs new cursor-based, with example request/response)
- Field naming/casing changes and a note on response envelope changes if any (e.g. removing wrapper objects)
- Deprecation timeline guidance (how long v1 stays available, how to detect via headers)
- A migration checklist specific to endpoints
- Common pitfalls (e.g. hardcoded URLs, assuming stable ordering without cursor, forgetting pagination loop changes)

Keep it concrete and practical, around 300-500 words. Return just the Markdown section as your final output — that IS the deliverable, not a description of it.

## Authentication

### What changed and why

v1 authenticated every request with a static `X-API-Key` header. These keys never expired, were typically shared across an entire team or service, and carried no notion of scope — a leaked key granted full account access indefinitely with no way to detect or limit the blast radius short of manual rotation.

v2 replaces this with **OAuth 2.0**. Server-to-server integrations use the **client credentials grant**; anything acting on behalf of a user uses the **authorization code grant** (with PKCE recommended for public/native clients). Instead of a permanent key, clients receive a short-lived JWT **access token** (typically 15–60 minutes) plus a longer-lived **refresh token**. This makes credentials revocable, scoped to specific permissions, and self-limiting in time — a stolen access token is only useful briefly, and refresh tokens can be revoked centrally without rotating a shared secret across every consumer.

### Request comparison

**v1:**
```bash
curl https://api.example.com/v1/orders \
  -H "X-API-Key: sk_live_51Hc8f9K2..."
```

**v2:**
```bash
curl https://api.example.com/v2/orders \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer eyJhbGciOiJSUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9..."
```

### Obtaining credentials

1. Register an application in the v2 Developer Portal (or `POST /v2/apps` for programmatic setup).
2. Choose a grant type: `client_credentials` for backend/server integrations, `authorization_code` for anything acting on a user's behalf.
3. Receive a `client_id` and `client_secret`. Store the secret in a vault/secrets manager — it replaces the old API key as your "root" credential and should never be committed to source control or shipped in a client binary.

### Token acquisition and refresh

```bash
curl -X POST https://api.example.com/v2/oauth/token \
  -d grant_type=client_credentials \
  -d client_id=$CLIENT_ID \
  -d client_secret=$CLIENT_SECRET \
  -d scope="orders:read orders:write"
```

Response:
```json
{
  "access_token": "eyJhbGciOi...",
  "token_type": "Bearer",
  "expires_in": 3600,
  "refresh_token": "def502...",
  "scope": "orders:read orders:write"
}
```

When `access_token` expires (check `expires_in`, don't wait for a 401), exchange the refresh token:
```bash
curl -X POST https://api.example.com/v2/oauth/token \
  -d grant_type=refresh_token \
  -d refresh_token=$REFRESH_TOKEN \
  -d client_id=$CLIENT_ID \
  -d client_secret=$CLIENT_SECRET
```

### Scopes and permissions

v2 tokens carry explicit scopes (e.g., `orders:read`, `orders:write`, `users:admin`) instead of the all-or-nothing access a v1 key implied. Request only the scopes your integration needs; the authorization server will reject or downgrade grants that exceed what the client/app is approved for.

### Migration checklist

- Register a new v2 application and generate `client_id`/`client_secret`
- Replace all `X-API-Key` header logic with `Authorization: Bearer <token>`
- Implement token acquisition (client credentials or auth code flow)
- Implement proactive refresh before expiry (don't rely on 401-triggered retries alone)
- Store `client_secret` and refresh tokens in a secrets manager, not config files or env dumps in logs
- Request minimal scopes needed per integration
- Add revocation/rotation runbook for the new secrets
- Load-test token endpoint calls to avoid rate-limiting during high-concurrency refresh

### Common pitfalls

- **Not caching tokens**: requesting a new token on every API call will hit rate limits — cache and reuse until near expiry.
- **Clock skew**: validate/refresh with a buffer (e.g., refresh at 90% of `expires_in`) to avoid edge-of-expiry failures.
- **Secret sprawl**: treat `client_secret` with the same care as a database password — never log it, never embed it in mobile/SPA clients (use auth code + PKCE there instead).
- **Ignoring `refresh_token` rotation**: some deployments issue a new refresh token on each use and invalidate the old one — always persist the latest one returned.

## Endpoints

### Base URL & Versioning

v1 endpoints were served from the bare API root with no version marker (e.g. `https://api.example.com/getUser`). v2 introduces explicit path-based versioning and a dedicated base URL:

- **v1:** `https://api.example.com/...`
- **v2:** `https://api.example.com/v2/...`

Clients should also send `Accept: application/vnd.example.v2+json` where supported, allowing content negotiation independent of the URL during transition.

### Endpoint Mapping (representative examples)

| Action | v1 | v2 |
|---|---|---|
| Get single user | `GET /getUser?id=123` | `GET /v2/users/123` |
| List users | `GET /user_list` | `GET /v2/users` |
| Create user | `POST /createUser` | `POST /v2/users` |
| Update user | `POST /updateUser` | `PATCH /v2/users/{id}` |
| Delete user | `POST /deleteUser?id=123` | `DELETE /v2/users/{id}` |
| List a user's orders | `GET /getOrdersForUser?uid=123` | `GET /v2/users/123/orders` |

The pattern: verbs move out of the path and into the HTTP method; resources are always plural nouns; identifiers move into the path, not the query string.

### Pagination

v1 used inconsistent, non-standard `offset`/`limit` (or `page`) query params with no forward-stability guarantee. v2 standardizes on cursor-based pagination:

**v1 request:** `GET /user_list?offset=40&limit=20`

**v2 request:** `GET /v2/users?limit=20&cursor=eyJpZCI6NDB9`

**v2 response:**
```json
{
  "data": [ { "id": "41", "firstName": "Ana" }, ... ],
  "pagination": { "nextCursor": "eyJpZCI6NjB9", "hasMore": true }
}
```
Loop termination changes from `offset += limit` to following `nextCursor` until `hasMore: false`. Do not compute cursors manually or assume they are numeric/decodable — treat them as opaque tokens.

### Field Naming & Response Envelope

v1 mixed `snake_case` and `camelCase` across endpoints (e.g. `user_id`, `createdAt`). v2 standardizes on **camelCase** for all JSON fields, and drops v1's inconsistent wrapper objects (e.g. `{"result": {"user": {...}}}`) in favor of a flat, predictable envelope: `{"data": {...}, "meta": {...}}` for single resources, `{"data": [...], "pagination": {...}}` for lists.

### Deprecation Timeline

- v1 remains available for **12 months** post-v2 launch, then read-only for 3 months, then retired.
- Deprecated v1 responses include `Deprecation: true` and `Sunset: <date>` headers — check for these programmatically rather than relying on documentation dates.

### Endpoint Migration Checklist

- [ ] Replace all hardcoded v1 URLs with `/v2/...` equivalents
- [ ] Convert verb-style calls to method + noun-resource calls
- [ ] Replace `offset`/`limit` loops with `cursor`/`hasMore` loops
- [ ] Update field access from snake_case/mixed to camelCase
- [ ] Remove code that unwraps old nested envelopes
- [ ] Monitor `Deprecation`/`Sunset` response headers in production

### Common Pitfalls

- Hardcoding full v1 URLs in client SDKs instead of using a configurable base URL.
- Assuming stable row ordering or reusability of `offset` after data mutates mid-pagination.
- Forgetting to update pagination loop exit conditions (checking `hasMore` instead of an empty array or offset overflow).
- Reading fields by old snake_case names after the response body has changed casing.

### What changed and why

v1 authenticated every request with a static `X-API-Key` header. These keys never expired, were typically shared across an entire team or service, and carried no notion of scope — a leaked key granted full account access indefinitely with no way to detect or limit the blast radius short of manual rotation.

v2 replaces this with **OAuth 2.0**. Server-to-server integrations use the **client credentials grant**; anything acting on behalf of a user uses the **authorization code grant** (with PKCE recommended for public/native clients). Instead of a permanent key, clients receive a short-lived JWT **access token** (typically 15–60 minutes) plus a longer-lived **refresh token**. This makes credentials revocable, scoped to specific permissions, and self-limiting in time — a stolen access token is only useful briefly, and refresh tokens can be revoked centrally without rotating a shared secret across every consumer.

```bash
curl https://api.example.com/v1/orders \
  -H "X-API-Key: sk_live_51Hc8f9K2..."
```

**v2:**
```bash
curl https://api.example.com/v2/orders \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer eyJhbGciOiJSUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9..."
```

1. Register an application in the v2 Developer Portal (or `POST /v2/apps` for programmatic setup).
2. Choose a grant type: `client_credentials` for backend/server integrations, `authorization_code` for anything acting on a user's behalf.
3. Receive a `client_id` and `client_secret`. Store the secret in a vault/secrets manager — it replaces the old API key as your "root" credential and should never be committed to source control or shipped in a client binary.

```bash
curl -X POST https://api.example.com/v2/oauth/token \
  -d grant_type=client_credentials \
  -d client_id=$CLIENT_ID \
  -d client_secret=$CLIENT_SECRET \
  -d scope="orders:read orders:write"
```

Response:

```json
  "access_token": "eyJhbGciOi...",
  "token_type": "Bearer",
  "expires_in": 3600,
  "refresh_token": "def502...",
  "scope": "orders:read orders:write"
}
```

When `access_token` expires (check `expires_in`, don't wait for a 401), exchange the refresh token:

```bash
  -d grant_type=refresh_token \

  -d client_id=$CLIENT_ID \
  -d client_secret=$CLIENT_SECRET
```

```json
  "token_type": "Bearer",
  "expires_in": 3600,
  "refresh_token": "def502...",
  "scope": "orders:read orders:write"
}
```

When `access_token` expires (check `expires_in`, don't wait for a 401), exchange the refresh token:
```bash
curl -X POST https://api.example.com/v2/oauth/token \
  -d grant_type=refresh_token \
  -d refresh_token=$REFRESH_TOKEN \
  -d client_id=$CLIENT_ID \
  -d client_secret=$CLIENT_SECRET
```

### Scopes and permissions

v2 tokens carry explicit scopes (e.g., `orders:read`, `orders:write`, `users:admin`) instead of the all-or-nothing access a v1 key implied. Request only the scopes your integration needs; the authorization server will reject or downgrade grants that exceed what the client/app is approved for.

### Migration checklist

- Register a new v2 application and generate `client_id`/`client_secret`
- Replace all `X-API-Key` header logic with `Authorization: Bearer <token>`
- Implement token acquisition (client credentials or auth code flow)
- Implement proactive refresh before expiry (don't rely on 401-triggered retries alone)
- Store `client_secret` and refresh tokens in a secrets manager, not config files or env dumps in logs
- Request minimal scopes needed per integration
- Add revocation/rotation runbook for the new secrets
- Load-test token endpoint calls to avoid rate-limiting during high-concurrency refresh

### Common pitfalls

- **Not caching tokens**: requesting a new token on every API call will hit rate limits — cache and reuse until near expiry.
- **Clock skew**: validate/refresh with a buffer (e.g., refresh at 90% of `expires_in`) to avoid edge-of-expiry failures.
- **Secret sprawl**: treat `client_secret` with the same care as a database password — never log it, never embed it in mobile/SPA clients (use auth code + PKCE there instead).
- **Ignoring `refresh_token` rotation**: some deployments issue a new refresh token on each use and invalidate the old one — always persist the latest one returned.

## Endpoints

### Base URL & Versioning

v1 endpoints were served from the bare API root with no version marker (e.g. `https://api.example.com/getUser`). v2 introduces explicit path-based versioning and a dedicated base URL:

- **v1:** `https://api.example.com/...`
- **v2:** `https://api.example.com/v2/...`

Clients should also send `Accept: application/vnd.example.v2+json` where supported, allowing content negotiation independent of the URL during transition.

### Endpoint Mapping (representative examples)

| Action | v1 | v2 |
|---|---|---|
| Get single user | `GET /getUser?id=123` | `GET /v2/users/123` |
| List users | `GET /user_list` | `GET /v2/users` |
| Create user | `POST /createUser` | `POST /v2/users` |
| Update user | `POST /updateUser` | `PATCH /v2/users/{id}` |
| Delete user | `POST /deleteUser?id=123` | `DELETE /v2/users/{id}` |
| List a user's orders | `GET /getOrdersForUser?uid=123` | `GET /v2/users/123/orders` |

The pattern: verbs move out of the path and into the HTTP method; resources are always plural nouns; identifiers move into the path, not the query string.

### Pagination

v1 used inconsistent, non-standard `offset`/`limit` (or `page`) query params with no forward-stability guarantee. v2 standardizes on cursor-based pagination:

**v1 request:** `GET /user_list?offset=40&limit=20`

**v2 request:** `GET /v2/users?limit=20&cursor=eyJpZCI6NDB9`

**v2 response:**
```json
{
  "data": [ { "id": "41", "firstName": "Ana" }, ... ],
  "pagination": { "nextCursor": "eyJpZCI6NjB9", "hasMore": true }
}
```
Loop termination changes from `offset += limit` to following `nextCursor` until `hasMore: false`. Do not compute cursors manually or assume they are numeric/decodable — treat them as opaque tokens.

### Field Naming & Response Envelope

v1 mixed `snake_case` and `camelCase` across endpoints (e.g. `user_id`, `createdAt`). v2 standardizes on **camelCase** for all JSON fields, and drops v1's inconsistent wrapper objects (e.g. `{"result": {"user": {...}}}`) in favor of a flat, predictable envelope: `{"data": {...}, "meta": {...}}` for single resources, `{"data": [...], "pagination": {...}}` for lists.

### Deprecation Timeline

- v1 remains available for **12 months** post-v2 launch, then read-only for 3 months, then retired.
- Deprecated v1 responses include `Deprecation: true` and `Sunset: <date>` headers — check for these programmatically rather than relying on documentation dates.

### Endpoint Migration Checklist

- [ ] Replace all hardcoded v1 URLs with `/v2/...` equivalents
- [ ] Convert verb-style calls to method + noun-resource calls
- [ ] Replace `offset`/`limit` loops with `cursor`/`hasMore` loops
- [ ] Update field access from snake_case/mixed to camelCase
- [ ] Remove code that unwraps old nested envelopes
- [ ] Monitor `Deprecation`/`Sunset` response headers in production

### Common Pitfalls

- Hardcoding full v1 URLs in client SDKs instead of using a configurable base URL.
- Assuming stable row ordering or reusability of `offset` after data mutates mid-pagination.
- Forgetting to update pagination loop exit conditions (checking `hasMore` instead of an empty array or offset overflow).
- Reading fields by old snake_case names after the response body has changed casing.

## Error Handling

### What Changed and Why

In v1, error responses were inconsistent: some endpoints returned a bare string, others `{"error": "..."}`, and some returned HTTP 200 with an error embedded in the response body. Status codes were also reused loosely (e.g., 400 for both validation failures and auth issues). This made programmatic error handling brittle — clients had to inspect body shape and string-match messages to figure out what went wrong.

v2 standardizes on correct HTTP status codes paired with a single, consistent JSON error envelope. Every error response includes a machine-readable `code`, a human-readable `message`, optional `details` for field-level validation errors, and a `request_id` for support and tracing. This makes errors predictable to parse, safe to branch on programmatically, and far easier to debug and support.

### Old vs New

**v1 (inconsistent):**
```json
"Invalid email address"
```
or
```json
{ "error": "not found" }
```
or (HTTP 200 with embedded error)
```json
{ "success": false, "error": "rate limit exceeded" }
```

**v2 (standardized envelope):**
```json
{
  "error": {
    "code": "validation_error",
    "message": "One or more fields failed validation.",
    "details": [
      { "field": "email", "issue": "must be a valid email address" }
    ],
    "request_id": "req_9f2c3a1b"
  }
}
```

### Common Error Codes

| HTTP Status | `code` | When It Occurs |
|---|---|---|
| 400 | `validation_error` | Request body/params fail schema or business-rule validation |
| 401 | `unauthorized` | Missing, invalid, or expired credentials |
| 403 | `forbidden` | Authenticated but lacking permission for the resource/action |
| 404 | `not_found` | Resource does not exist or is not visible to the caller |
| 409 | `conflict` | Request conflicts with current resource state (e.g., duplicate, version mismatch) |
| 429 | `rate_limited` | Client exceeded allowed request rate |
| 500 | `internal_error` | Unexpected server-side failure |

### Rate Limiting

v2 responses include `X-RateLimit-Limit`, `X-RateLimit-Remaining`, and `X-RateLimit-Reset` headers on all requests. When a `429 rate_limited` is returned, a `Retry-After` header (seconds) indicates when to retry.

### Retry Guidance

- **Safe to retry (with backoff):** `429 rate_limited`, `500 internal_error`, and network/timeout errors. Use exponential backoff with jitter; honor `Retry-After` when present.
- **Do not retry blindly:** `400 validation_error`, `401 unauthorized`, `403 forbidden`, `404 not_found`, `409 conflict` — these indicate the request itself needs correction, not transient failure. Retrying unchanged will fail again.
- Cap total retry attempts (e.g., 3–5) and use idempotency keys for retried writes.

### Migration Checklist

- [ ] Parse errors from the `error` envelope, not from top-level or ad hoc fields.
- [ ] Branch on `error.code`, never on `error.message` text.
- [ ] Stop checking HTTP 200 bodies for embedded error flags — treat any non-2xx status as authoritative.
- [ ] Log `request_id` alongside client-side errors for support correlation.
- [ ] Update retry logic to respect status-code-based rules and `Retry-After`.
- [ ] Surface `details` for validation errors in UI instead of generic messages.

### Common Pitfalls

- Continuing to poll for `success: false` in a 200 body instead of trusting the status code.
- String-matching on `error.message` (localized/free text) rather than the stable `error.code`.
- Retrying non-idempotent requests on 409/400 without inspecting the cause.
- Ignoring `request_id` in logs, making support escalations slower to diagnose.
